p.src: Now Yang Yi heard that troops were blocking the road ahead. He hurriedly sent scouts, who returned to report that Wei Yan had burned down the plank roads and led troops to bar the way. Yang Yi was greatly alarmed and said, “While the Chancellor lived, he foresaw that this man would eventually rebel. Who would have thought it would truly happen today? Now that he has cut off our road home, what are we to do?” Fei Yi said, “He must already have fabricated a memorial to the Emperor, falsely accusing us of rebellion. That is why he burned the plank roads and blocked our return. We too must submit a memorial to the Emperor, setting forth the facts of Wei Yan’s rebellion, and then devise a way to deal with him. Jiang Wei said, “There is a narrow path here called Chashan. Though rugged and precipitous, it will allow us to circle around behind the plank road. Let us write a memorial to inform the Emperor while at the same time leading the troops along the Chashan path.”

He awoke in terror and sat waiting for dawn; then he assembled his civil and military officials at court to interpret the dream. Qiao Zhou said, “Last night I looked up and observed the heavens. I saw a red star with hornlike rays fall from northeast to southwest. It portends a grave calamity for the Chancellor. Your Majesty’s dream of a mountain collapsing corresponds precisely to this omen.” The Latter Ruler grew still more frightened. Suddenly it was reported that Li Fu had arrived, and the Latter Ruler urgently summoned him and questioned him. Li Fu bowed his head to the ground and tearfully reported that the Chancellor had died. He then recounted in detail everything the Chancellor had said before his death. On hearing this, the Latter Ruler wept bitterly and cried, “Heaven has destroyed me!” He collapsed weeping upon the imperial couch. The attendants supported him into the inner palace. p.src: When the Empress Dowager had heard it, she asked, “What is your judgment of the matter?” Jiang Wan memorialized, “In my humble judgment, although Yang Yi is by nature excessively impatient and intolerant of others, he has long worked with the Chancellor in calculating provisions and assisting with military plans. Now that the Chancellor entrusted him with this great responsibility at the point of death, he is certainly not a man who would rebel. Wei Yan has always relied upon his achievements and sought to stand above others, while everyone yielded to him. Yang Yi alone would make no concessions, and Wei Yan came to hate him. Now, seeing Yang Yi placed in command of the army, he refused to submit. He therefore burned the plank roads, cut off Yang Yi’s route home, and then falsely accused him in a memorial, seeking to bring about his ruin. I pledge every member of my household, high and low, as surety that Yang Yi will not rebel; but I truly dare not vouch for Wei Yan.” Dong Yun also memorialized, “Wei Yan, trusting in his great achievements, has always harbored resentment and uttered words of complaint. The only reason he did not rebel before was that he feared the Chancellor. Now that the Chancellor has just died, it is inevitable that he should seize the opportunity to make trouble. As for Yang Yi, he is able and quick-witted and was trusted and employed by the Chancellor; he certainly would not rebel.” The Latter Ruler said, “If Wei Yan has indeed rebelled, what plan should we use to resist him?” Jiang Wan said, “The Chancellor had long suspected this man and must have left a plan with Yang Yi. If Yang Yi had nothing to rely upon, how could he have withdrawn into the mouth of the valley? Wei Yan is certain to fall into the trap. Your Majesty, set your mind at ease.” Before long, another memorial arrived from Wei Yan, again declaring that Yang Yi had rebelled. While it was being read, another memorial arrived from Yang Yi, declaring that Wei Yan had rebelled. The two men submitted memorials one after another, each arguing his own right and the other’s wrong. Suddenly it was reported that Fei Yi had arrived. The Latter Ruler summoned him, and Fei Yi reported the circumstances of Wei Yan’s rebellion in detail. The Latter Ruler said, “If that is so, let Dong Yun for the present bear the imperial tally and go to reason with him, soothing him with conciliatory words.” Dong Yun received the edict and departed.

p.src: Meanwhile, He Ping led his troops straight to the rear of the Southern Valley, where they beat the drums and raised a mighty shout. Mounted scouts sped to report to Wei Yan that Yang Yi had ordered his vanguard He Ping to lead troops around by the Chashan path and challenge him to battle. Wei Yan flew into a rage, hurriedly donned his armor, mounted his horse, and led his troops out with blade in hand to meet them. When the two armies had drawn up opposite each other, He Ping rode forward and shouted abuse: “Where is the rebel Wei Yan?” Wei Yan shouted back, “You are helping Yang Yi rebel! How dare you curse me?” He Ping rebuked him: “The Chancellor has only just died, and his bones are not yet cold. How dare you rebel!” Then, raising his whip and pointing toward the troops of Shu, he said, “You soldiers are all men of Western Sichuan. In Sichuan many of you have parents, wives and children, brothers, kinsmen, and friends. While the Chancellor lived, he never treated you poorly. You must not now aid a rebel. Each of you should return to your native place and await your reward.” When the soldiers heard this, they gave a great shout, and more than half dispersed. Wei Yan was enraged. Brandishing his blade, he spurred his horse straight at He Ping. He Ping leveled his spear and rode out to meet him. After only a few bouts, He Ping feigned defeat and fled, with Wei Yan in pursuit. The troops loosed their bows and crossbows together, forcing Wei Yan to turn his horse and retreat. Seeing his troops breaking and fleeing in disorder, Wei Yan’s anger turned upon them. He spurred after them and killed several men, but still could not stop the rout. Only the three hundred men commanded by Ma Dai remained in place. Wei Yan said to Ma Dai, “You have aided me with true devotion. When our enterprise succeeds, I shall certainly not fail you.” He then joined Ma Dai in pursuing He Ping. He Ping led his troops away at full speed. Wei Yan gathered the remnants of his army and consulted Ma Dai, saying, “What if we defect to Wei?” Ma Dai said, “Your words, General, are most unwise. Why should a true man not carve out a dominion for himself, instead of lightly bending the knee to another? As I see it, you possess both wisdom and courage in abundance. Who among the warriors of the Two Riverlands would dare oppose you? I swear to join you in first taking Hanzhong and then advancing to conquer the Two Riverlands.”

p.src: Wei Yan was overjoyed and, together with Ma Dai, led his troops straight toward Nanzheng. From the walls of Nanzheng, Jiang Wei saw Wei Yan and Ma Dai advancing in a mighty, swaggering tide. Jiang Wei hurriedly ordered the drawbridge raised. Wei Yan and Ma Dai shouted, “Surrender at once!” Jiang Wei sent for Yang Yi and consulted him: “Wei Yan is fierce, and Ma Dai is helping him besides. Though his troops are few, by what stratagem can we drive him back?” Yang Yi said, “As the Chancellor lay dying, he left behind a silk pouch and instructed me: ‘If Wei Yan rebels, open this only when you face him before a city; within is a plan to slay him.’ Now we should take it out and see.” He took out the silk pouch and broke its seal, only to find written within: “Do not open this until you face Wei Yan in battle, mounted on horseback.” Jiang Wei was delighted. “Since the Chancellor left such precise instructions, you, Chief Clerk, should keep it in your possession. I shall first lead the troops out of the city and draw them up in formation; then you may come forth.” Jiang Wei donned his armor, mounted his horse, and took his spear in hand. Leading three thousand soldiers, he opened the city gate and charged out with them as one. Drums thundered as they formed their battle lines. Jiang Wei leveled his spear and reined in beneath the command banner, shouting abuse at the top of his voice: “Wei Yan, you traitor! The Chancellor never treated you unjustly. Why have you rebelled today?” Wei Yan held his saber crosswise and reined in his horse. “Boyue, this has nothing to do with you. Just send Yang Yi out here!” In the shadow of the command banner, Yang Yi opened the silk pouch and read the instructions within. Overjoyed, Yang Yi rode out lightly armed, halted before the battle line, pointed at Wei Yan, and laughed: “While the Chancellor lived, he knew that you would one day rebel and told me to guard against you. Now his words have indeed come true. If you dare shout ‘Who dares kill me?’ three times in succession from horseback, then you are a true man of valor. I shall then surrender the city of Hanzhong to you.” Wei Yan laughed loudly. “Listen well, you wretch Yang Yi! While Kongming lived, even I feared him somewhat. Now that he is dead, who under Heaven dares oppose me? Never mind three times—even thirty thousand would be no hardship!” He raised his saber, gathered the reins, and shouted from horseback, “Who dares kill me?” Before he had finished the first cry, a man behind him answered fiercely, “I dare kill you!” His arm rose and his saber fell, striking Wei Yan dead beneath his horse. All who saw it were appalled. The man who slew Wei Yan was none other than Ma Dai. It turned out that, as Kongming lay dying, he had secretly entrusted Ma Dai with a plan: he was to wait until Wei Yan uttered that challenge, then take him unawares and cut him down. When Yang Yi had finished reading the strategy in the silk pouch that day, he knew Ma Dai had been planted at Wei Yan’s side. He therefore followed the plan, and Wei Yan was duly slain. The Latter Emperor issued a decree: “Since his guilt has already been clearly established and punished, let his former services nevertheless be remembered. Sun Quan’s expression darkened, and he said, “Wu and Shu have become one family. Why, then, has your sovereign reinforced the defenses at Baidi?”

Zong Yu replied, “In my view, that the east should reinforce its garrison at Baqiu and the west its defenses at Baidi is merely what circumstances require. Neither side need question the other about it.”
Sun Quan laughed. “You are no whit inferior to Deng Zhi.”

u.src: Then he said to Zong Yu, “Since hearing that Chancellor Zhuge has ascended to Heaven, I have shed tears every day and ordered all my officials to wear mourning.
I feared that the men of Wei might take advantage of your mourning to seize Shu, so I added ten thousand defenders at Baqiu to serve as reinforcements. I had no other intention.”
Zong Yu bowed his head to the ground in thanks.
Sun Quan said, “Since I have pledged an alliance, how could I possibly betray that bond of honor?”
Zong Yu said, “Because the Chancellor has only recently died, the Son of Heaven specially commanded me to come and announce his passing.”
Sun Quan then took a gold-tipped arrow and broke it in two, swearing, “If I betray our former alliance, may my line be extinguished!”
He also ordered an envoy to carry incense, silk, and funeral offerings into Shu to perform the rites.

p.src: Zong Yu took leave of the ruler of Wu and returned to Chengdu with the Wu envoy. Appearing before the Latter Emperor, he reported: “Upon the Chancellor’s recent death, the ruler of Wu himself shed tears and ordered all his ministers to wear mourning. He reinforced Baqiu only because he feared the men of Wei would exploit our weakness and invade; he harbors no other designs. He has now broken an arrow in oath and will not betray the alliance.” The Latter Emperor was delighted. He rewarded Zong Yu lavishly and treated the Wu envoy with great generosity before sending him on his way. Then, in accordance with Kongming’s final instructions, he appointed Jiang Wan Chancellor and General-in-Chief, with authority over the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat. Fei Yi was appointed Prefect of the Masters of Writing and charged to manage the Chancellor’s affairs jointly with him. Wu Yi was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, granted the imperial staff, and placed in command of Hanzhong. Jiang Wei was appointed General Who Assists Han and Marquis of Pingxiang, with overall command of the troops in every region; together with Wu Yi, he was stationed at Hanzhong to guard against the armies of Wei. All the remaining officers retained their former posts.

p.src: Yang Yi considered himself senior to Jiang Wan both in age and official service, yet found himself placed beneath him. Moreover, relying on the greatness of his own achievements and resentful that he had received no rich reward, he complained to Fei Yi: “When the Chancellor first died, had I led the entire army over to Wei, would I now be left in such obscurity?” Fei Yi secretly submitted a full account of these words to the Latter Emperor. The Latter Emperor was furious. He ordered Yang Yi cast into prison and interrogated, intending to execute him. Jiang Wan memorialized: “Though Yang Yi is guilty, he rendered much meritorious service while following the Chancellor in past days. He should not be executed, but reduced to commoner status.” The Latter Emperor accepted this counsel and demoted Yang Yi, sending him to live as a commoner in Jia Commandery in Hanzhong. Overcome with shame, Yang Yi cut his own throat and died.

Now Cao Rui, ruler of Wei, appointed Sima Yi Grand Commandant, placing him in overall command of the armed forces and charging him with securing the frontiers. Sima Yi bowed his thanks and returned to Luoyang. The ruler of Wei, residing in Xuchang, embarked on vast building works and raised official halls and palaces; in Luoyang he also constructed the Chaoyang and Taiji Palaces and built the Zongzhang Tower, each a hundred feet high; he further erected the Chonghua Palace, Qingxiao Pavilion, Phoenix Tower, and Nine-Dragon Pool, ordering the erudite Ma Jun to oversee the work. Their magnificence was unsurpassed: carved beams and painted rafters, green-glazed tiles and golden bricks, all glittering brilliantly in the sun. p.src: Cao Rui read the memorial and angrily exclaimed, “Does Dong Xun not fear death?” His attendants petitioned that Dong Xun be beheaded. Cao Rui said, “This man has always been loyal and righteous, so for now I shall merely strip him of office and reduce him to commoner status. But whoever speaks such reckless words again shall surely be put to death!” At that time Zhang Mao, styled Yancai, an attendant to the crown prince, likewise submitted a memorial of earnest remonstrance, and Cao Rui ordered his execution.” That very day he summoned Ma Jun and said, “I am building lofty terraces and towering pavilions so that I may commune with the immortals and seek the secret of eternal youth and life.” Ma Jun memorialized, “Of the twenty-four emperors of the Han, Emperor Wu alone reigned the longest and attained the greatest span of life. This was because he imbibed the essence of the sun and the radiance of the moon from heaven. He once built the Bailiang Terrace within the palace at Chang'an; upon it stood a bronze figure holding a basin in its hands, called the Dew-Receiving Basin. At the third watch it caught the pure vaporous water descending from the Northern Dipper, known as the ‘Celestial Nectar’ and also as ‘Sweet Dew.’ If one grinds fine jade, mixes it with this water, and drinks it, one may cast off age and regain youth.” Cao Rui was overjoyed and said, “Take laborers to Chang'an this very night, dismantle the bronze figure, and move it into Fanglin Park.”

p.src: Ma Jun accepted the command and led ten thousand men to Chang'an, where he ordered wooden scaffolding erected all around so that they might ascend the Bailiang Terrace. Before long, five thousand men climbed in spirals, hauling themselves up by linked ropes and cables. The Bailiang Terrace was two hundred feet high, and the bronze pillar measured ten arm-spans around. Ma Jun ordered them first to dismantle the bronze figure. Many men joined their strength and brought the bronze figure down, whereupon they saw tears streaming from its eyes. Everyone was greatly alarmed. Suddenly a violent wind arose beside the terrace, sending sand and stones flying as fiercely as a driving rain; with a tremendous crash like heaven and earth splitting asunder, the terrace tilted and its pillars collapsed, crushing more than a thousand men to death. Ma Jun took the bronze figure and golden basin back to Luoyang, entered the ruler of Wei's presence, and presented the bronze figure and Dew-Receiving Basin. The ruler of Wei asked, “Where is the bronze pillar?” Ma Jun replied, “The pillar weighs a million jin and could not be transported here.” Cao Rui ordered the bronze pillar broken into pieces and transported to Luoyang, where it was cast into two bronze figures called ‘Wengzhong’ and set outside the Sima Gate; he also had a bronze dragon and phoenix cast: the dragon stood forty feet high and the phoenix more than thirty, and both were placed before the palace. p.src: Now Lady Mao, Cao Rui's consort, was a native of Henei; in earlier years, when Cao Rui was Prince of Pingyuan, they had been deeply devoted to one another; and when he ascended the imperial throne, she was installed as—; later, however, Cao Rui favored Lady Guo, and Lady Mao fell from favor. Lady Guo was beautiful and clever, and Cao Rui doted on her. He took his pleasure with her every day and did not leave the inner palace for more than a month. In the third month of spring that year, when a hundred flowers vied in bloom throughout Fanglin Park, Cao Rui went there with Lady Guo to admire them and drink wine. Lady Guo said, “Why not invite the empress to share our pleasure?” Cao Rui replied, “If she were here, not a single drop would pass my throat.” He then instructed the palace maids that Lady Mao must not be allowed to learn of it. Lady Mao, seeing that Cao Rui had not entered her principal palace for more than a month, went that day with over ten palace women to the Cuihua Tower to divert herself. Hearing strains of music ringing out, she asked, “Where is that music being played?” A palace officer reported, “His Majesty and Lady Guo are admiring the flowers and drinking wine in the imperial garden.” On hearing this, Lady Mao was distressed at heart and returned to her palace to rest. The next day Lady Mao rode out from the palace in a small carriage. Meeting Cao Rui in a winding gallery, she smiled and said, “Your Majesty's excursion to the northern park yesterday must have been a great delight!” Cao Rui flew into a rage. He immediately had all who had attended him the previous day seized and brought before him, then rebuked them: “When I visited the northern park yesterday, I forbade those around me to let Lady Mao know. How was it disclosed after all?” He shouted an order that the palace officers behead every one of the attendants. Lady Mao was horrified and turned her carriage back to her palace. Cao Rui at once issued an edict granting Empress Mao death and installed Lady Guo as empress. None of the court officials dared remonstrate. Then one day Guanqiu Jian, Inspector of Youzhou, submitted a memorial reporting that Gongsun Yuan of Liaodong had rebelled, proclaimed himself King of Yan, inaugurated the first year of the Shaohan era, built palaces, appointed a palace administration, and raised troops to invade the borders, throwing the north into turmoil. Cao Rui was greatly alarmed and immediately assembled his civil and military officials to discuss a plan for raising an army to repel Gongsun Yuan. Indeed:
